Commentary.Commentary: Back for the chase. The Aussie openers - Phoebe Litchfield and Alyssa Healy are out in the middle. The Indians have taken their place as well. Kranti Gaud to bowl first.
....THE CHASE...

Right then, the spotlight shifts to Australia’s batters. A target of 282 won’t be going that easily against India’s spin quartet, but it’s certainly chaseable on this good batting surface. Can India’s bowlers defend this total with early breakthroughs, or will Australia’s top order stroll through to another clinical chase? The chase is in a bit, so don't go anywhere!

Pratika Rawal of India Women is up for a quick chat. She says that it is a decent total and is confident that they’ll defend. Tells that it is a no-brainer to say that she and Smriti Mandhana enjoy batting together. Reckons that the pitch was on a slower side due to the drizzle happening during the match, and that could be the reason for the slower run rate. Mentions that they need to find early wickets and contain runs. Admits that they have an amazing spin side, and the pacers are in good form as well.

Australian bowlers? Credit where due. After being smashed around in the first 20 overs, they regrouped brilliantly. Megan Schutt was the pick of the lot, with 2/45 in her seven overs, breaking India’s backbone in the middle. King’s flight earned her the wicket of Rawal, while Sutherland and McGrath chipped in with crucial strikes. Kim Garth kept things tight in her full quota. It has been a classic Australian fightback - absorb the punches, then hit back with discipline.

But then came Harleen Deol, after struggling early, to the rescue. Harleen played positively, striking 54 off 57 balls, but her wicket at 207 threatened to undo India’s recovery. Then Richa Ghosh brought the spark, although fortune favoured her when she was reprieved on 6 after McGrath’s No-Ball. She made the Aussies pay with a quick-fire 25 off 20 balls, before Ash Gardner took a well-judged catch. The final flourish came from Radha Yadav and Deepti Sharma, who ensured India closed in on the 280-mark.

What went wrong in the middle overs? Rawal, who started fluently, lost momentum and consumed 96 balls for her 64 before being undone by Alana King. Harmanpreet, eager to make her landmark match memorable, fell LBW to Annabel Sutherland after just 11 runs. Pressure mounted as dot balls piled up, and Australia sensed an opening. Jemimah Rodrigues, too, couldn’t convert her start, dismissed by Tahlia McGrath. At 161/3 in the 34th over, India’s acceleration looked uncertain.

Harmanpreet Kaur, in her 150th ODI, won the toss and batted first, and her openers did exactly what was needed. Smriti Mandhana and Pratika Rawal were off to a good start, racing to 55 in the first Powerplay without losing a wicket. Both looked assured, registering their half-centuries and played stylish strokes. But just when India looked set for domination, a mix-up between the two ended Mandhana’s classy knock of 58, a self-inflicted run out against the run of play. From 114/1 in the 22nd over, the innings began to stutter.

281 on the board - good score? Who would be the happier side at the break? Surely Australia, who after being hammered early by India’s top order, clawed their way back and restricted the hosts to a total that looks modest on this batting-friendly Mullanpur surface. India, meanwhile, will be a touch disappointed, as with the platform they had, 300-plus looked certain, but losing wickets at crucial intervals pulled them back. Still, this is a good score, and with India’s experienced bowling attack at home, the match is finely poised for now.

Commentary.Commentary: Done with the pre-match formalities! The crowd has come in good numbers for the first international match hosted here at the Maharaja Yadavindra Singh International Cricket Stadium. We can see the Australia Women side in a huddle before they spread out to take their respective field positions. Pratika Rawal and Smriti Mandhana are the two openers for India Women. Megan Schutt has the new ball in her hand on her 100th ODI. Let's play...

We are not far away from the start of the game, but before that, we see the players from both sides make their way out to the middle and line up for the respective national anthems. It will be Australia's first, followed by the national anthem of India.

PITCH REPORT - Deep Dasgupta says that it is a good batting deck. Adds that there are a few cracks, but the batters will enjoy playing here and there will be a few later on. Mentions that the square boundaries are 66 and 68 meters, while the straight hit is 69 meters. Ends by saying that it is a high-scoring ground.

Smriti Mandhana, the vice-captain of the India Women, is up for a quick chat before the start of play. Speaking about preparations, she shares that the build-up has been good, with a fitness-based camp in Bengaluru followed by a solid camp in Visakhapatnam, where the team will also be playing a few games. On the team’s progress ahead of the marquee event, she recalls that the England tour was positive, with several youngsters stepping up and performing well. However, she emphasises that it is in the past, and the focus now is on moving forward. With three ODIs before heading straight into the World Cup, she notes that the team cannot dwell too much on what happened in England, but admits it was a good tour overall.

India Women (Playing XI) - Smriti Mandhana, Pratika Rawal, Harleen Deol, Harmanpreet Kaur (C), Jemimah Rodrigues, Richa Ghosh (WK), Deepti Sharma, Sneh Rana, Sree Charani, Radha Yadav, Kranti Gaud.

Alyssa Healy, the captain of the Australia Women, says she is not too bothered and is happy to bowl first. Hopes the ball slides onto the bat nicely. Reckons she was out of action for nine months but is looking forward to being in India for the next six-seven weeks. Mentions they haven't played much white-ball lately, but they love playing this format. Feels they could try a few combinations in this series. Informs that Darcie Brown, Sophie Molineux, Grace Harris, and one other are not playing in this game.

The skipper of the India Women, Harmanpreet Kaur, says that they will BAT first. On completing her 150th ODI, she reflects that it has been a great journey, and she feels very fortunate to represent India, hoping to continue for a few more years. Speaking about the wicket, she feels that it looks like a good batting surface and wants to post a big total in the first innings. On the team combination, she informs that they are going in with four spinners and one pacer.
TOSS - The coin lands in favour of Harmanpreet Kaur and India Women have elected to BAT first.

Australia Women, led by Alyssa Healy, arrive as favourites with a strong record in women's cricket. The team's batting lineup, featuring players like Beth Mooney and Phoebe Litchfield, provides stability. Their attack, led by Megan Schutt and Alana King, will test India's batters. Schutt is likely to become the ninth Australian to feature in 100 Women's ODIs in the first match. Sophie Molineux, who has recovered from injury, is unlikely to feature in the playing XI during the series but is being groomed for the upcoming World Cup as she is seen as a key player for the future. All in all, Australia Women are the favourites on paper but India Women are coming high on confidence with a good record at home lately. When the world’s cricketing superpower meets the world’s cricketing dreamers, sparks are bound to fly. India Women, desperate to shed their tag of perennial runners-up, face Australia Women, the seven-time world champions, in the first ODI of the three-match series at the Maharaja Yadavindra Singh International Cricket Stadium in Mullanpur. With the 2025 ODI World Cup around the corner, both sides will treat this series as more than just warm-ups - to fine-tune combinations, test nerves, and send an early message. For Indian Women, it’s about belief. For Australian women, it’s about maintaining their aura. What does this match mean for India? Can they finally turn promise into silverware? For the India Women, this is not just a trial run, as it’s an opportunity. India have never lifted an ODI World Cup, and the build-up to the 2025 edition is filled with both hope and scrutiny. Renuka Singh Thakur’s return from injury strengthens their pace attack, while Amanjot Kaur’s absence for this series gives them a chance to test the balance without her. With Kranti Gaud impressing as the highest wicket-taker against England in July 2025, and spin depth through Sneh Rana and Sree Charani, India’s bowling suddenly looks more rounded than it has in years. But what about India’s batting? Smriti Mandhana and youngster Pratika Rawal are likely to open, as both are in form and both are capable of giving fiery starts. Harleen Deol at No. 3 has been consistent, while the experienced trio of Harmanpreet Kaur, Jemimah Rodrigues, and Richa Ghosh provides firepower in the middle. But can India’s middle order withstand Australia’s pressure? That’s the real test. Losing Yastika Bhatia to injury is a blow, but Uma Chetry’s inclusion means they still have flexibility behind the stumps. India’s focus will be on sharpening their finishing power - something they’ve lacked in crunch games. Meanwhile, what about the Australian side? How have they shaped up? Australia walk in like they always do - calm, confident, and world-beaters by default. Alyssa Healy, fresh off a 137 unbeaten against India A, will lead with bat and gloves. Beth Mooney and Ellyse Perry remain pillars, while Tahlia McGrath adds all-round strength. Their biggest challenge? Managing injuries. Sophie Molineux is still recovering from knee surgery and is unlikely to feature in this series, but she’ll be back for the World Cup. Georgia Wareham has recovered in time, adding more spin firepower. Any surprise picks or talking points for Australia? Yes, Grace Harris returns, and her big-hitting middle-order role could be crucial, especially in Indian conditions, while Georgia Voll is another exciting addition. Australia’s selectors have also drafted in Nicole Faltum and Charli Knott for the India ODIs as experience-building options. The question is - can Australia keep their streak against India alive? Last time India toured Australia in December 2024, they swept India 3-0. Overall, the head-to-head reads 46-10 in Australia’s favour. Clearly, history leans heavily their way. So, what can we expect? The Maharaja Yadavindra Singh International Cricket Stadium is relatively new, but word is the pitch offers pace with carry - meaning the ball should come nicely onto the bat. But the ground is big, so six-hitting won’t be easy, and running between the wickets will matter. Spinners might come into play later in the innings. With India trying to prove themselves and Australia looking to sharpen their dominance, expect a fierce contest. Who holds the edge? On paper, Australia. They have the trophies, the pedigree, and the psychological edge. But cricket isn’t played on paper. India, with home advantage, returning stars, and a burning desire to end their drought, will see this as a chance to shake up the narrative. One side looks to stay invincible. The other side looks to become unforgettable.
